annotation.title_clean: Autonomous Surgical Robots: The Malpractice-Product Liability Boundary
annotation.title_en: Autonomous Surgical Robots: The Malpractice-Product Liability Boundary
annotation.summary_en: Journal article proposing the Autonomy-Control-Risk Attribution (ACRA) framework to decide when harm from autonomous surgical robots falls under medical malpractice, product liability, or concurrent liability, based on meaningful human control, risk provenance and informational control, avoiding surgeons becoming a moral crumple zone.
key_provisions_or_claims: Where clinicians retain effective control, malpractice should remain the primary regime.
Harm from hardware, software, algorithms or warnings clinicians cannot detect or control shifts weight to product liability.
Distributed control warrants concurrent liability rather than a single doctrinal category.
ACRA assesses autonomous function, meaningful control, risk provenance, informational control and interaction failures.
Surgeons should not become a moral crumple zone for machine decisions.
